turns.t: Doctor, I just don't get it. I've got a whole bag of pills, and nobody ever tells me what half of them are for.
That's exactly what we're here to sort out today, Dorothy. And I see Marcus has come along with you.
Morning. I'm her carer, I come in every morning and set up the pill organizer for the week.
Wonderful. Marcus, how many different medicines is she taking at this point?
Eleven, the last time I counted. I brought the whole bag in case you want to go through it.
Good thinking, we'll get to the bag in a minute. First, how have you been feeling, Dorothy?
Oh, I'm fine, mostly. I'm just wiped out a lot of the time.
Wiped out. Is that all day long, or worse at certain times?
Worse in the afternoons. By three o'clock I'm like a wet dishrag.
And when did the wiped out feeling start, roughly?
Oh, gosh. Was it before Christmas? Or maybe after? I really couldn't tell you.
I can't pin it down either. It sort of crept up on both of us.
That's fine, it doesn't need an exact date. Are you getting dizzy at all, Dorothy?
No, not me. I'm not dizzy.
Well, she is, though. She gets dizzy when she stands up fast. Twice last week I had to grab her arm.
Oh, Marcus, that's nothing. I just got up too quick.
Let's keep that in mind. I'd like to check your pressure sitting down, and then again standing up.
All right, whatever you need.
Sitting, your blood pressure is 134 over 78, and your pulse is 72.
Now stand up nice and slowly for me, and I'll take it once more.
Standing, it comes down to 108 over 66.
Is that bad? I feel perfectly okay standing here.
It's a bigger drop than I'd like. My best guess is that the combination of tablets is pushing your pressure down when you stand up.
That would explain why I keep having to catch her.
It might. Let me ask about a few other things. How about your breathing, any trouble there?
No, that's fine. Breathing's been fine.
Good. And what conditions have you been carrying around over the years?
Oh, high blood pressure, for ages. And the arthritis in my knees. That one's a real pain.
Okay. And you're at home on your own, is that right?
Yes, I live on my own. Marcus comes by every morning, bless him.
Every day but Sunday.
Alright. Here's what I'd like to do. I'll order a blood test to check how your kidneys and salts are doing.
Do I have to fast for it?
No need to. Marcus, the lab will take her whenever it suits you both.
Sure, I can run her over there.
In the meantime, Dorothy, when you get up from a chair or bed, sit for a moment first, then stand slowly.
Sit first, then stand. I can manage that.
And Marcus, please keep giving everything exactly as you have been until I've gone over that whole bag properly.
Will do. Thank you, doctor.
Thank you. I feel better knowing somebody's actually looking at it all.
You're very welcome. Take care, both of you.

Keep giving all medicines as before until the full list is reviewed

Neither patient nor carer can say when the tiredness began.
